items.title: Why you forget English words and how to fix it
items.text: Many students try to memorize English words and feel frustrated when they forget them. They repeat vocabulary again and again, but the effect is temporary . The issue isn’t memory. It is the learning strategy. Words without context are difficult to keep. The brain needs connections to store information effectively. Stories create those connections. They give words meaning and show how they work in real situations. When you listen to a story and imagine it, you engage your brain fully. You connect the words to real pictures in your head. LangoPlay applies this method in a simple way. It offers short, interactive stories where you listen, think, and respond. Each step increases your understanding and helps you remember. Over time, the difference is clear. You keep vocabulary longer and use it more confidently. If you want to stop forgetting words, stop relying on memorization. Start learning through stories and build memory that lasts. Start to play LangoPlay today. You can start for free. Go to www.langoplay.com . Difficult words: temporary (not for a long time), engage (activate), increase (make bigger).

items.title: Good news of October
items.text: A roundup of positive global developments highlights encouraging progress across conservation, medicine, and technology. Environmental reports reveal that deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon dropped significantly, and lead to the lowest fire activity in decades, while wild tigers returned to Kazakhstan after 70 years. In Canada, Indigenous nations partnered with the federal government to establish a massive marine reserve. Medical breakthroughs feature a world-first eye implant that restores vision for patients with age-related macular degeneration , a fast 10-second liquid treatment stopping tooth decay in children, and a new mRNA flu vaccine showing improved effectiveness. Meanwhile, global public health initiatives reached historic milestones. HIV infections have fallen to a 30-year low, and digital tracking helps health workers vaccinate over 200,000 previously unreached children in Nigeria. Finally, European regulations now require digital watermarks on AI, and global electric vehicle sales surged to nearly 30 percent of total market share. Difficult words: implant (a medical device, tissue, or object that is placed inside the body through surgery), macular degeneration (an eye disease that causes vision loss in the center of the field of vision as people age), watermark (a hidden or visible digital mark in a file or image to identify its source). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Good news of October
items.text: This month brings positive news from around the world in nature, health, and clean technology. Amazon deforestation dropped by nearly 40 percent, and reduced forest fires, while wild tigers were returned to Kazakhstan. In Canada, Indigenous communities teamed up with the government to protect a huge ocean area. In health news, a tiny eye implant approved in Europe helps bring back lost vision , and a fast liquid treatment stops tooth decay in young children without drilling. Also, global HIV infections dropped to their lowest level in 30 years, and new digital tracking helped health teams vaccinate 200,000 children in Nigeria. Lastly, European laws now want clear labels on AI videos, and electric cars made up almost 30 percent of new global car sales. Difficult words: deforestation (cutting down forests and trees across a wide area), implant (a tiny piece of medical equipment placed inside the body to help it work), vision (the ability to see things with your eyes), decay (damage to your tooth). items.title: Good news of October
items.text: There is good news from around the world today! People cut down fewer trees in the Amazon rainforest, and wild tigers return to Kazakhstan. Canada makes a big sea park to save fish and ocean life. Doctors make many great improvements . A small new eye tool helps sick people see again. A quick liquid stops tooth pain in children. Health workers also help 200,000 children get vaccines in Nigeria. Also, new European rules say that AI videos must have clear labels. Another good news is that almost 30 percent of new cars in car shops are now electric. Difficult words: return (to come back), improvement (a change which makes something better), liquid (a substance which flows freely, like water or oil). items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. It cited the International Council of Museums' Code of Ethics, which says museums "should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Man sells everything for AI dream "partner"
items.text: A man in Brazil had a sad experience in his search for love. Mr X, 49, sold everything he owned to get enough money to see a woman he met online. He travelled over 2,000 kilometres by bus. He first met her online in 2020 and fell in love with her. He wanted to marry her. Her name was Jessica. Her online profile read: "I really want to support you. I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life." Mr X went to meet her in the city of Belo Horizonte, but he could not find her. He showed people photos of her, but nobody knew who she was. He then found out that she was not real. She was created by AI. The man was sad. He said: "I came here to find happiness." Mr X's story shows how risky it can be to look for love online. Many people feel lonely and want to find a partner. However, they can be easily tricked because AI can make people who look and sound real. Jessica's social media account had over 300,000 followers. She looked like a real woman. The person who created Jessica said they made her to get people's attention online. They wanted to use the AI Jessica to help sell things. Mr X wants people to be careful so they don't make a similar mistake in the future. It is important to check the identity of a person you meet online carefully. items.title: One billion meals thrown away every day
items.text: More than one billion meals are thrown away worldwide every day, despite famine and millions of people starving. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) recently reported that households are responsible for 60 per cent of food waste, followed by restaurants and food services at 28 per cent, and shops at 12 per cent. The Maldives has the highest estimated household food waste per person, at around 260 kilograms annually. Syria, Seychelles, Mexico and Tunisia also recorded high levels. Globally, food waste accounts for 8 to 10 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions. As discarded food decomposes in landfills, it releases the dangerous greenhouse gas methane, which accelerates global warming. Individuals, businesses and governments can all take practical steps to reduce food waste. People should plan meals, prepare shopping lists, and purchase only what they need. We should store ingredients correctly and freeze surplus portions. We should also turn leftovers into new dishes and compost inedible waste. Restaurants and supermarkets also have a huge part to play in reducing food loss. They can donate surplus food to communities in need. Martin Krause, Director of the Climate Change Division at UNEP, said: "Every meal rescued, shared or never wasted is food put to better use." items.title: Made in Qatar
items.text: Qatar is actively expanding its national production to diversify its economy and build a strong global reputation for homegrown brands. Local agricultural and food companies are leading this movement by boosting food security through fully integrated, sustainable farming systems. For example, major local producers have increased fresh poultry supply to meet almost all domestic demand while developing zero-waste operations powered by solar energy and recycled water. At the same time, health-conscious entrepreneurs are introducing plant-based foods and cold-pressed juices to fill gaps in the market. Beyond agriculture, strategic investment firms are supporting unique industrial ventures , including the country’s first electric vehicle factory. Together, these initiatives show how Qatar is moving beyond its traditional energy sector. The country empowers local talent and creates high-quality, sustainable products capable of competing on the international stage. Difficult words: reputation (the opinion that people generally have about how good, reliable, or successful someone or something is), entrepreneur (a person who starts and runs their own business), venture (a new business activity or project). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Made in Qatar
items.text: Qatar is working hard to create its own products and build strong local businesses. The country wants to rely less on oil and increase its national food security . Local farming companies now produce fresh chicken, eggs, and dairy for almost the whole population. They use modern, eco-friendly methods like solar power and water recycling. Also, young business owners are making healthy plant-based foods, juices, and snacks. They are planning to sell them to neighboring countries soon. Qatar is also investing in new technology, such as building its first electric car factory. Through these green initiatives , companies are supporting local talent, creating new jobs, and showing the world that their homegrown products offer great quality and sustainability . Difficult words: food security (when people have enough good food), initiative (an important new plan or action), sustainability (using natural resources in a way which doesn’t harm the planet). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Made in Qatar
items.text: Qatar is making many new things at home. Local farms are producing fresh milk, eggs, and meat. People do not have to buy food from other countries. These farms use clean sun power and recycle water to stay green . Small companies are also making healthy juices and plant-based food for schools and shops. They want to sell their food to other countries soon. The country is even building a factory to make electric cars. People in Qatar are happy to buy local goods. They create new jobs and help their country grow. Difficult words: green (good for the planet), plant-based (from plants, not animals), local (from a specific area or country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea
items.text: The British government has approved drilling at a controversial North Sea gas field, despite strong opposition from environmental groups. Energy companies welcomed the decision and predicted the project could supply over six percent of the nation’s gas at peak production. Officials argue that developing domestic resources is necessary to boost national energy security while global conflicts drive up fuel costs. The prime minister stated that although the country remains committed to long-term climate targets, oil and gas will still be needed during the transition to renewable energy. However, climate activists and politicians heavily criticized the approval and warned that increased fossil fuel reliance won’t lower household energy bills because prices are dictated by international markets. They stress that true security requires a faster shift toward clean energy rather than expanding fossil fuel infrastructure. Difficult words: controversial (causing a lot of angry public discussion and strong disagreement), dictate (to state, order, or control authoritatively how something must be done or decide), reliance (dependence on someone or something for help or support). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea
items.text: The UK government approved a new project to drill for gas in the North Sea. Energy companies say this project will help produce more gas for the country. Leaders argue that using local gas makes the country safer as global conflict causes energy prices to rise. The prime minister explained that the country still needs gas while moving toward green energy. Environmental groups and green politicians strongly disagree with the plan. They warn that drilling produces harmful emissions and will not lower electricity bills for normal families. Activists argue that the government should focus on renewable energy like wind and solar instead of fossil fuels. Difficult words: approve (to officially agree), harmful (when something hurts living things or the planet), renewable energy (energy from natural sources, such as wind, sun, and so on). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: The UK says yes to drilling in the North Sea
items.text: The UK government says yes to getting new gas from under the sea. There is a plan to drill in the North Sea. Leaders say that this gas will help keep the country safe when energy prices are high. The prime minister says that the country still needs gas, but it also wants clean energy in the future. Many people are very angry about this decision . They say that getting more gas is bad for the planet. It will not help people get cheaper electricity. They want the government to use clean power like wind and sun instead of oil and gas. Difficult words: drill (to make a hole in the earth to get oil or gas), price (how much money something costs), decision (what you do after thinking or talking about it). items.title: Salmon farming and tech
items.text: Salmon farming is a growing, multi-billion-dollar industry. The biggest producers, Norway and Chile, have seen booming profits; however, the industry is facing problems such as mass salmon die-offs, infectious diseases, and environmental damage. Fish farming relies heavily on chemicals and antibiotics to treat parasites that can weaken or kill the fish. A large farm in Norway, Norlock, uses freshwater baths and chemical treatments to combat salmon lice, but these methods can also stress the fish and lead to further health issues. One innovative solution at Norlock involves using laser technology to remove the parasites, reducing infection rates. Also, farms in open sea environments benefit from ocean currents, which can help wash away waste and reduce diseases. Chile’s salmon farms, which are heavily dependent on antibiotics, are also under scrutiny for their environmental impact. New methods like closed aquaculture systems, which keep farmed fish in tanks and prevent contamination, offer hope for a more sustainable future in salmon farming. Difficult words: parasite (an organism that lives in or on an organism and feeds from it), innovative (featuring new methods), scrutiny (critical and detailed examination).
